frequency_question: How often does structural friction (inter-agency vetoes, systemic financial stability concerns, or diplomatic pushback) successfully block the actual execution of threatened major secondary sanctions against systemically important foreign banks?
membership_rule: Includes formal U.S. executive branch deliberations or credible statutory threats regarding secondary financial sanctions against Tier-1 foreign banks from major geopolitical adversaries over energy trade since 2010. Excludes minor Tier-3/4 institutions where waivers are routine.

cases.name: 2012 NDAA Iran sanctions implementation against Chinese small/medium banks
CAATSA secondary sanctions threats against Turkish/European entities
Section 311/PATRIOT Act actions against major international correspondent banking nodes for North Korea/Iran
Executive Order 14024 secondary sanctions authorizations for Russian energy/financial intermediaries

coverage_note: 4 major historical clusters examined where structural friction was actively tested against systemic targets.
known_gaps: Classified internal deliberations where potential secondary sanctions were dropped entirely before public threat phase are unobservable.
skeleton: Total credible high-stakes secondary sanction threats against major systemic foreign financial institutions versus instances where structural friction (Treasury/State/NSC interagency pushback on systemic blowback) caused a retreat or waiver.
multiplier: 4 evaluated major escalation cycles, yielding 3 actual implementations of severe penalties and 1 waiver/deferral due to systemic friction.
validity_reason: The institutional architecture of U.S. secondary sanctions enforcement and inter-agency friction points remain stable across typical presidential administration cycles.
